source_title: Restrictions on Use of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (privacy/surveillance)
uas_topic: Privacy / unauthorized surveillance and photography by UAS
regulated_party: Any person, entity, or State agency
regulated_activity: Conducting surveillance of a person/dwelling/curtilage or private real property without consent; photographing an individual without consent for publication/public dissemination
requirement_type: Prohibition, with law-enforcement and emergency-management exceptions
summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.1(b) prohibits any person, entity, or State agency from using a UAS to (1) conduct surveillance of a person or a dwelling and its curtilage without consent, or of private real property without the owner's/easement holder's/lessee's consent, or (2) photograph an individual without consent for the purpose of publishing or publicly disseminating the photograph (with an exception for newsgathering, newsworthy events, or events/places open to the general public). Law enforcement agencies have five listed exceptions (subsection (c)), including counter-terrorism determinations, plain-view surveillance, search warrants, exigent circumstances, and photographing public gatherings; an emergency management agency exception (subsection (c1)) covers incident command, reconnaissance, search and rescue, damage assessment, hazard risk management, and floodplain mapping. A person whose privacy is violated has a civil cause of action with statutory damages of $5,000 per photograph/video, plus costs and attorney's fees (subsection (e)); evidence obtained in violation is generally inadmissible in criminal prosecutions (subsection (f)).
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Routine AEC aerial mapping, inspection, and construction-progress photography over a project site is not the conduct this statute targets, but avoid incidental surveillance-style capture of neighboring private property, dwellings, or individuals without consent — adjust flight paths or camera settings near residential areas bordering a project site.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This statute creates a private civil cause of action with statutory damages ($5,000 per image/video) distinct from any criminal exposure — document the professional/survey purpose and project boundary of any flight near residential property, and obtain consent where the flight path may reasonably capture private property or individuals outside the project scope.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against the North Carolina General Assembly's official codified-statutes website.

geographic_scope: Statewide, with local-government carve-out for locally owned property
source_title: Regulation of Launch and Recovery Sites
uas_topic: Launch/recovery site consent requirement; local-government regulatory authority over own property
regulated_activity: Launching or recovering a UAS from State or private property without consent; local governments may separately regulate launch/recovery from their own property
requirement_type: Consent requirement (state/private property); local ordinance authority (local government property)
permit_or_approval_required: No (consent from property owner/controller, not a government permit, for state/private land generally)
public_agency_only: Partial — local governments only, as to their own property
summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.2(a) prohibits launching or recovering a UAS from any State or private property without consent. Subsection (b) separately authorizes a unit of local government to adopt an ordinance regulating the use of the local government's own property for UAS launch or recovery — this is the primary statutory basis for local UAS ordinances in North Carolina, and it is narrower than a general local police-power grant: it applies only to the local government's own property, not to UAS operation generally within its jurisdiction.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Obtain documented consent from the property owner or controlling State agency before launching or recovering a UAS from any State-owned or private property outside the client's own project site; separately check whether a specific municipality has adopted a locally-owned-property launch/recovery ordinance (e.g., a city park) if the project involves local-government land.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This statute is the primary hook for North Carolina's (narrower, property-based) local UAS ordinance authority — distinguish it for clients from a broad local police-power grant; a full local-ordinance survey for locally owned property near a specific project site is a later research-phase task.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against NCDOT's official summary document, which reproduces the statute word-for-word from the ratified act.

geographic_scope: Statewide (500 ft horizontal / 250 ft vertical buffer around confinement/correctional facilities)
source_title: Use of an Unmanned Aircraft System Near a Confinement or Correctional Facility Prohibited
regulated_party: Any person, entity, or State agency
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS within 500 ft horizontal / 250 ft vertical of a local confinement facility or State/federal correctional facility
requirement_type: Prohibition, with a written-consent defense and a narrower commercial/public-utility exception
permit_or_approval_required: No — but a narrower distance/notice regime applies to public utilities and commercial entities (see summary)
public_agency_only: Yes, for public utilities/providers/commercial entities meeting the statutory conditions
summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.3(a) prohibits operating a UAS within a horizontal distance of 500 ft or vertical distance of 250 ft from any local confinement facility (as defined in G.S. 153A-217) or State/federal correctional facility, measured outward from the facility's exterior walls, perimeter fences, or a marked boundary with notices posted no more than 100 yards apart. Subsection (b) provides exceptions for: (1) a person with written consent from the official in responsible charge of the facility; (2) a law enforcement officer acting under § 15A-300.1(c); and (3) a public utility, § 146-29(a)(6) provider, or commercial entity that (a) stays outside a narrower 150 ft horizontal/150 ft vertical buffer, (b) gives the facility's responsible official at least 24 hours' notice (commercial entities compliant with § 15A-300.1 are exempt from this notice requirement), (c) uses the UAS for utility/provider infrastructure inspection or other business purposes, (d) operates for commercial purposes in compliance with FAA rules and Chapter 63, Article 10, and (e) does not physically enter the prohibited space without a facility escort. Emergency management agencies, EMS, firefighters, and law enforcement are exempt when responding to an emergency. Penalties range from a Class I misdemeanor ($500 fine) for a bare violation, up to a Class H felony ($1,500 fine) for delivering or attempting to deliver a weapon, or a Class I felony ($1,000 fine) for delivering or attempting to deliver contraband. Violating UAS are subject to law-enforcement seizure and forfeiture.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This is directly relevant to any AEC infrastructure-inspection or mapping work near a North Carolina jail or prison — a commercial AEC operator inspecting nearby utility infrastructure may be able to use the narrower 150 ft/150 ft commercial exception (with 24-hour notice) rather than needing outright facility consent, but confirm the exact facility boundary and posted-notice markings on site, and document FAA Part 107 compliance since that is a condition of the commercial exception.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Do not assume general FAA Part 107 certification alone satisfies this statute — the commercial exception requires meeting all five listed conditions (150 ft buffer, 24-hour notice or § 15A-300.1 compliance, qualifying business purpose, FAA/Chapter 63 Article 10 compliance, and no unescorted entry); document each element given the felony exposure tied to weapon/contraband delivery, and note that Chapter 63, Article 10 (referenced in condition (d)) was substantially repealed effective Dec. 1, 2024 (see NC-009) — confirm what compliance with 'Article 10' now requires in light of that repeal.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against NCDOT's official summary document, which reproduces the statute word-for-word from the ratified act (S.L. 2017-179); note the statute's own commercial-exception condition (d) cross-references Chapter 63, Article 10, which was substantially repealed in 2024 — see NC-009 for that unresolved interaction.
notes: High-priority item: confirm with NCDOT's Division of Aviation how the 2024 repeal of Chapter 63, Article 10's permit/test requirements affects the 'compliance with Article 10' condition in § 15A-300.3(b)(3)(d), since that cross-reference may now point to a largely repealed article.

geographic_scope: Statewide (3,000 ft horizontal/vertical buffer around an active forest fire)
issuing_authority: North Carolina General Assembly / North Carolina Forest Service
source_title: Use of an Unmanned Aircraft System Near a Forest Fire Prohibited
regulated_party: Any person, entity, or State agency
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS within 3,000 ft horizontal or vertical distance of any forest fire within North Carolina Forest Service jurisdiction
requirement_type: Prohibition, with consent, law-enforcement, and Forest Service exceptions
summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-300.4(a), enacted in 2023, prohibits operating a UAS within a horizontal or vertical distance of 3,000 ft from any forest fire within North Carolina Forest Service jurisdiction, measured outward from the fire's or fire-control lines' furthest exterior perimeter. Exceptions (subsection (b)) apply to a person with consent from the official in responsible charge of the fire, a law enforcement officer acting under § 15A-300.1(c), and Forest Service employees/those acting under their direction. Penalties are unusually severe and tiered by consequence: up to a Class D felony if the violation proximately causes another person's death, down to a Class A1 misdemeanor for a violation not otherwise covered, each carrying a mandatory minimum $1,000 fine; a Class G or H felony applies specifically where the violation interferes with emergency operations. Violating UAS are subject to law-enforcement seizure and forfeiture.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: This statute is directly relevant to any AEC post-wildfire damage assessment or infrastructure-inspection work — do not fly within 3,000 ft of an active forest fire without first obtaining consent from the official in charge of managing that fire, given the unusually severe, injury-tiered felony exposure (up to Class D felony if death results).
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the specific consent obtained from the Forest Service or incident-command official before any flight near an active or recently active forest fire; this is one of the most severely penalized state UAS statutes reviewed to date and warrants conservative compliance given the felony exposure tied to interference with emergency operations even absent injury.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against the North Carolina General Assembly's official codified-statutes website.

summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 14-280.3 makes it a Class H felony for a person to willfully damage, disrupt the operation of, or otherwise interfere with a manned aircraft through use of a UAS, while the manned aircraft is taking off, landing, in flight, or otherwise in motion.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Maintain airspace awareness and situational deconfliction near any active manned-aircraft operations (agricultural aviation, helicopter utility work, medevac, etc.) during AEC UAS flights, since willful interference carries felony exposure.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: This is a willfulness-based felony statute distinct from ordinary FAA airspace-deconfliction rules — document standard operating procedures for detecting and yielding to manned aircraft as evidence against any willfulness allegation.

source_title: Unlawful Possession and Use of Unmanned Aircraft Systems (weapon attachment; hunting/fishing)
regulated_activity: Possessing or using a UAS with a weapon attached; using a UAS to fish or hunt
summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 14-401.24(a) makes it a Class E felony to possess or use a UAS with a weapon attached. Subsection (b) makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor to fish or hunt using a UAS. Subsection (d) clarifies the section does not prohibit possession or use of a UAS authorized by federal law or regulation.

regulated_activity: Publishing or disseminating recorded images taken by infrared or similar thermal imaging technology attached to a UAS, revealing individuals/materials/activities inside a structure, without the property owner's consent
summary: N.C. Gen. issuing_authority: North Carolina General Assembly / Wildlife Resources Commission
source_title: Unlawful Harassment of Persons Taking Wildlife Resources (UAS-specific provision)
regulated_activity: Using a UAS to interfere with the lawful taking of wildlife resources, or to drive, harass, or intentionally disturb wildlife resources for the purpose of disrupting lawful taking
summary: N.C. Gen. Stat. § 113-295(a1) makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor to use a UAS to violate subsection (a) of the same section, which independently prohibits intentionally interfering with the lawful taking of wildlife resources or driving/harassing/intentionally disturbing wildlife resources for the purpose of disrupting lawful taking (subsection (a) itself, without a UAS, is a Class 2 misdemeanor for a first offense and Class 1 for subsequent offenses). The Wildlife Resources Commission may separately seek civil injunctive relief, including attorney's fees and expert-witness costs.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Plan environmental-monitoring, habitat-mapping, or resource-inventory UAS flights to avoid any activity that could be read as disrupting the lawful taking of wildlife resources, with a conservative standoff buffer near active hunting/fishing areas during relevant seasons.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Document the survey/mapping purpose of any UAS flight over wildlife habitat or areas of active lawful hunting/fishing to distinguish it from a prohibited harassment/disruption use.
verification_status: Full current statutory text verified directly against NCDOT's official summary document, which reproduces the statute word-for-word from the ratified act.

issuing_authority: North Carolina Department of Transportation, Division of Aviation / North Carolina General Assembly
source_title: Repeal of State UAS Knowledge Test and Commercial Operator Permit Requirement
citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. §§ 63-95, 63-96 (Chapter 63, Article 10) — REPEALED by S.L. 2024-15, s. 21(a)
regulated_party: Commercial and government UAS operators previously required to hold a State permit
public_agency_only: No — this was a requirement that has been eliminated, which is favorable for commercial operators
aec_relevance: High (significant favorable change for AEC compliance burden)
summary: Effective December 1, 2024, Session Law 2024-15 (House Bill 198, enacted after the General Assembly overrode a gubernatorial veto) repealed Article 10 of Chapter 63 of the General Statutes, eliminating the separate North Carolina UAS knowledge test and the State commercial-operator permit requirement (formerly codified at §§ 63-95 and 63-96) that had applied on top of FAA Part 107 certification. As of this repeal, commercial and government UAS operators in North Carolina need only comply with FAA Part 107 (or other applicable federal authorization) and are not required to separately hold a State-issued UAS permit or pass the State knowledge test.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not plan for or advise clients to obtain a North Carolina State UAS commercial-operator permit or complete the State knowledge test — this requirement no longer exists as of December 1, 2024. FAA Part 107 certification remains the operative commercial licensing requirement.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Update any pre-December-2024 compliance checklists or client-facing materials that referenced the North Carolina UAS permit or knowledge test, since those requirements have been repealed; note that § 15A-300.3(b)(3)(d) (NC-003) still cross-references 'Chapter 63, Article 10' compliance as a condition of its commercial correctional-facility exception, creating an unresolved interpretive question about what that cross-reference now requires post-repeal.
verification_status: Repeal and effective date confirmed directly against NCDOT's own official Laws & Regulations webpage (last updated 12/6/2024) and corroborated by contemporaneous industry news coverage (dronelife.com, ncaerox.com) of the veto override and Session Law 2024-15.
notes: This is a high-value, recent (2024) change that materially reduces the North Carolina-specific compliance burden for commercial AEC UAS operators compared to the pre-2024 regime; flag prominently for any client previously operating under the old permit system.

summary: 07 NCAC 13B .1204 prohibits a person from voluntarily bringing, landing, causing to descend or alight, ascending, or taking off within or upon any North Carolina Division of Parks and Recreation property with a UAV or drone (along with other named aviation apparatus), except under authorization of a Special Activity or Special Use Permit obtained under 07 NCAC 13B .0104. issuing_authority: North Carolina Board of Examiners for Engineers and Surveyors (NCBELS); U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit
source_title: Unlicensed-Surveying Enforcement Against Drone Mapping/Photogrammetry Operators — 360 Virtual Drone Services LLC v. Ritter
citation: N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 89C (Engineering and Land Surveying Act); 360 Virtual Drone Services LLC v. Ritter, 102 F.4th 263 (4th Cir. 2024), cert. denied Apr. 20, 2026
source_type: Binding law or regulation; binding federal appellate court decision
effective_date: Chapter 89C: ongoing; 4th Cir. decision: 2024-05-20 (cert. denied 2026-04-20, now final)
revision_date: 2026-04-20 (Supreme Court cert. denial made the 4th Circuit ruling final)
status: Current / in force -- MATERIALLY EXPANDED in this retrofit pass (see notes)
uas_topic: Unlicensed-practice-of-land-surveying enforcement against drone mapping, photogrammetry, orthomosaic imaging, 3D modeling, and volumetric/elevation data services
regulated_party: Any person or business offering UAS-derived mapping/photogrammetry products or services, licensed or not
regulated_activity: Providing a client with a drone-derived orthomosaic map, 3D digital model, elevation data, distance/volume measurements, or geospatial-metadata-tagged aerial photography -- NCBELS treats this as the unlicensed practice of land surveying if the provider is not a licensed PE/PLS, regardless of whether the provider claims to establish legal boundaries
requirement_type: License (PE or PLS) required, per NCBELS enforcement position upheld by the 4th Circuit
permit_or_approval_required: License required (not a permit) unless the deliverable falls outside NCBELS's asserted scope
summary: MATERIALLY EXPANDED 2026-08-07: the prior version of this record understated a significant, currently binding risk. NCBELS does not merely lack UAS-specific guidance -- it has actively and repeatedly enforced against small-business drone operators since 2018, issuing cease-and-desist letters to at least a half-dozen companies for practicing land surveying without a license. In the best-documented case, NCBELS investigated and formally warned Michael Jones (360 Virtual Drone Services LLC, Goldsboro, NC) that his orthomosaic mapping, thermal imaging, and geospatial-metadata photography services constituted unlicensed surveying under Chapter 89C, regardless of whether he claimed to establish legal boundaries. Jones sued on First Amendment grounds; the Fourth Circuit ruled for NCBELS on May 20, 2024 (360 Virtual Drone Services LLC v. Ritter, 102 F.4th 263), holding the Board may restrict non-licensees' communication of maps and 3D digital models under a 'loosened' First Amendment standard for occupational speech. The U.S. Supreme Court denied certiorari on April 20, 2026, making the Fourth Circuit's ruling final. Per NCBELS's own stated enforcement position (as described in the litigation record), providing a client with any of the following without a PE/PLS license risks unlicensed-practice enforcement: aerial photographs containing geospatial metadata or coordinate/distance information; orthomosaic maps; 3D digital models from photogrammetry; elevation/topographic products; or rough distance or stockpile-volume measurements from processed aerial imagery. Chapter 89C's general competency-in-practice requirement (for licensed PEs/PLS themselves) remains a separate, narrower point within this same statutory framework.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat any UAS-derived deliverable containing geospatial metadata, coordinates, distances, elevations, volumes, or an orthomosaic/3D model as presumptively within NCBELS's asserted licensing scope, per the now-final Fourth Circuit ruling -- route such deliverables through a licensed North Carolina PE or PLS regardless of whether the product purports to establish legal boundaries. Do not assume a disclaimer avoids the licensing requirement; NCBELS's enforcement position does not turn on whether boundary lines are claimed.
practical_interpretation_uas_procurement: N/A — no procurement or equipment-selection implication identified
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Advise clients that this is an active, currently enforced, and now judicially settled risk in North Carolina -- not a hypothetical gap. Confirm licensure status before a non-licensed operator delivers any mapping/photogrammetry product with the characteristics NCBELS has targeted, and consider the Fourth Circuit's now-final ruling (cert. denied April 2026) when assessing a First Amendment defense, since that avenue is foreclosed in this Circuit.
verification_status: N.C. Gen. Stat. Chapter 89C's general framework re-confirmed via ncleg.gov. The 360 Virtual Drone Services LLC v. Ritter litigation history, enforcement pattern, and outcome were verified directly against the Institute for Justice's case page (which represented the plaintiff and links the Fourth Circuit's own opinion), corroborated by Justia's case-law reproduction of the same Fourth Circuit opinion (102 F.4th 263, decided 2024-05-20) and Casemine/vLex case citations. IJ's own April 20, 2026 press release confirms the Supreme Court's certiorari denial.
notes: MATERIAL CHANGE 2026-08-07: this record previously said only 'no standalone Board rule... was located,' which significantly understated the real risk -- NCBELS has actively enforced since 2018 and won a binding Fourth Circuit precedent, now final after Supreme Court cert. denial. This is arguably the single most consequential finding of this state's retrofit for the AEC audience this project serves. Recommend direct verification of NCBELS's current published enforcement/guidance position (21 NCAC 56) for the specific deliverable characteristics of a given engagement.
